name: Ezra
bio:
Ezra, a priest descended from Aaron through Seraiah, Azariah, and Hilkiah, was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses who had devoted himself to studying and obeying the LORD's law and teaching it in Israel. In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes of Persia, with the LORD's hand upon him, Ezra led a group of Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants from Babylon to Jerusalem, departing on the first day of the first month and arriving on the first day of the fifth month.

Artaxerxes gave Ezra a sweeping letter of authorization: any Israelites who wished could return with him; he was to carry silver and gold freely given by the king, his counselors, and the people of Babylon for the temple and use it for offerings and whatever else seemed good to him and his fellow Israelites; the royal treasurers beyond the Euphrates were to supply him with silver, wheat, wine, oil, and salt on request, up to generous limits; temple personnel were exempted from taxation; and Ezra was to appoint magistrates and judges to teach and enforce God's law, with serious penalties for those who disobeyed. Ezra blessed the LORD for moving the king's heart this way and for showing him favor before the king and his officials, and, strengthened by God's hand on him, gathered leading men of Israel to go up with him (Ezra 7:1-28).

 At the river Ahava, Ezra found no Levites among the returnees and sent for ministers from Iddo at Casiphia, who supplied Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and others. Rather than ask the king for a military escort — ashamed to, after telling him God's hand favored all who sought him — Ezra proclaimed a fast there to seek a safe journey for the people, their children, and their possessions. He then entrusted the temple's silver, gold, and vessels to twelve chief priests, including Sherebiah and Hashabiah, charging them to guard the holy offering until it could be weighed out again in Jerusalem. The company departed the Ahava safely, arrived in Jerusalem unharmed, delivered the treasure, and offered burnt offerings for all Israel (Ezra 8:1-36).

 Soon after, Jewish leaders reported to Ezra that the people, priests, and Levites — officials chief among them — had intermarried with the surrounding peoples and adopted their abominable practices. Appalled, Ezra tore his clothes and hair and sat in stunned silence until the evening sacrifice, when he fell to his knees and prayed, confessing the nation's long history of guilt, acknowledging that God had already shown them undeserved mercy in letting a remnant survive and rebuild, and admitting that intermarrying with these peoples again would be to break God's clear command and risk total destruction (Ezra 9:1-15).

 As Ezra wept before the temple, Shechaniah son of Jehiel proposed that Israel covenant with God to send away the foreign wives and their children, urging Ezra to take charge; Ezra made the leaders swear to do it, then withdrew to Johanan son of Eliashib's chamber and fasted in his grief. He summoned all the returned exiles to Jerusalem on pain of forfeiture, and before the assembled, rain-soaked crowd declared their intermarriage a trespass and called them to separate from their foreign wives. The people agreed but asked for time, given their numbers and the weather, so family heads were appointed to handle each case before judges and elders. Over the following months, officials including Jonathan son of Asahel investigated the matter until every case was resolved, and the guilty — a substantial list spanning priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and ordinary Israelites — put away their wives (Ezra 10:1-44).

 With the wall finished, all the people gathered as one and asked Ezra to bring out the Book of the Law. Standing on a wooden platform built for the occasion, flanked by thirteen named officials, Ezra read it aloud from morning to midday before the whole assembly, who stood in reverence as he opened it and blessed the LORD; Levites moved through the crowd explaining the meaning as he read. When the people wept on hearing the Law's demands, Ezra joined Nehemiah and the Levites in telling them this was a holy, joyful day, not one for grief, and sent them off to feast and share with those in need. The next day, the leaders studying with Ezra discovered the Law's command to keep the Feast of Tabernacles, which the people then celebrated with tree branches and booths with greater joy than at any time since the days of Joshua son of Nun — Ezra read from the Law every day of the seven-day feast (Nehemiah 8:1-18).
